name: Petya and Array
description: Count the number of subarrays of an array (which may contain negative numbers) whose sum is strictly less than a given t.
why_hard: Negative elements break plain two-pointer/sliding-window counting, forcing the prefix-sum-plus-Fenwick-tree trick (count pairs of prefix sums within a range) — the standard escape hatch when two pointers fail.

name: Close Tuples (hard version)
description: Count the number of size-m subsequences of an array such that the difference between the maximum and minimum element in the subsequence is at most k.
why_hard: Requires sorting, then a two-pointer sliding window to bound each candidate "maximum" element's valid range, combined with nCr combinatorics to count subsequences per window — a clean fusion of two pointers with counting rather than plain search.

name: OpenStreetMap
description: Given an n×m grid, compute the minimum element of every k×k submatrix and sum all these minima.
why_hard: Naive per-submatrix scanning is too slow; it requires chaining a 1D sliding-window-minimum (monotonic deque) pass over rows and then over columns — a genuinely hard monotonic-structure sliding-window problem in 2D.

name: Subarray Sums II
description: Count the number of subarrays (of an array that may contain negative or zero values) with sum exactly equal to a given x.
why_hard: Unlike the "easy" version restricted to non-negative values (solvable with a simple two-pointer window), negative values invalidate the sliding-window monotonicity, forcing a prefix-sum + hashmap-of-counts approach.

name: Maximum Subarray Sum II
subtopic: Kadane variant with length constraint (prefix sums + segment tree/deque)
description: Find the maximum possible sum of a subarray whose length is between two given bounds a and b.
why_hard: Plain Kadane's algorithm doesn't enforce a length window, so this needs prefix sums combined with a sliding-window-of-minimums structure (segment tree or monotonic deque) over the valid range of earlier prefix indices — a substantially harder Kadane variant.

name: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum value in every contiguous window of size k as it slides across the array.
why_hard: The naive approach is O(nk); achieving O(n) requires maintaining a monotonic decreasing deque of indices, the canonical hard-sliding-window-with-monotonic-structure technique.

name: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
description: Given an integer array (possibly containing negative numbers) and integer K, find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray with sum at least K, or -1 if none exists.
why_hard: Negative numbers break simple two-pointer/Kadane approaches, so the intended solution keeps a monotonic increasing deque of prefix-sum indices and pops/pushes carefully — a non-obvious combination of prefix sums with a monotonic-deque sliding window.

name: Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target
description: Given a 2D matrix and an integer target, count the number of non-empty submatrices whose element sum equals target.
why_hard: Requires reducing the 2D problem to repeated 1D "subarray sum equals k" counting (via row-pair compression using 2D prefix sums) combined with hashmap counting — a genuine 2D-prefix-sum-and-difference-array-style trick, not a toy application.

name: Range Increments
description: Given the final array state (all elements start at 0), reconstruct the minimum number of `rangeIncrement(l, r)` calls (each adds 1 to every element in `[l, r]`) that could have produced it.
why_hard: It is the textbook difference-array problem — the answer is exactly the sum of positive jumps in the difference array, and reconstructing actual (l, r) calls requires a stack-based matching on top of the diff-array insight.

name: Too Many Segments (hard version)
description: Given n segments on a line and a limit k, remove the minimum number of segments so that no integer point is covered by more than k segments.
why_hard: Requires building a difference array of coverage counts, sweeping left to right, and greedily evicting the segment with the farthest right endpoint (via a multiset/heap) whenever the running coverage from the diff array exceeds k.

name: Clear the Multiset
description: Given counts a_1..a_n of a multiset containing a_i copies of value i, find the minimum number of operations (remove one occurrence of every value in a contiguous range, or remove x copies of one value) to empty the multiset.
why_hard: Generalizes the "min ops = sum of positive differences in the difference array" idea from Range Increments into a divide-and-conquer over the minimum value, making it a strong step up in difficulty while keeping the difference-array insight central.

name: Addition on Segments
description: Starting from an all-zero array, given q range-add operations (add x_i to [l_i, r_i]), determine every value y that the array maximum can equal after applying some subset of the operations.
why_hard: Combines difference-array range updates with a bitset subset-sum DP over "how much can the max at each position be pushed up", forcing you to reason about the interaction between range updates and reachability.

name: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal to Target
description: Given `nums` and `target` of the same length, find the minimum number of operations to turn `nums` into `target`, where one operation increments or decrements a contiguous subarray by 1.
why_hard: Direct generalization of the classic "minimum range-increment operations" difference-array problem to signed deltas, requiring you to track running sums of positive and negative jumps in the difference array of `target - nums`.

name: Array Partition
description: Split an array into three non-empty contiguous parts x, y, z such that max of the first part equals min of the second part equals max of the third part, or report impossible.
why_hard: Solved by scanning prefix/suffix max and min arrays with pointers that advance the boundary positions in one pass, an in-place multi-region partition search analogous to Dutch-flag-style boundary maintenance.

name: Range and Partition
description: Choose a value range [x, y] and split the array into k contiguous subarrays such that every subarray has strictly more elements inside [x, y] than outside, minimizing y − x.
why_hard: Requires partitioning the whole array into an "inside/outside" two-coloring driven by a chosen threshold range, then greedily walking the array with pointers to carve out valid subarrays — a direct extension of two-way in-place partitioning.

name: Recover the Original Array
description: Given an array formed by interleaving `arr[i]-k` and `arr[i]+k` for an unknown k, recover a valid original array `arr`.
why_hard: After sorting, you must partition the multiset into a "low" group and a "high" group that are a perfect k-shifted match of each other, using a two-pointer/multiset scan that mirrors the low/high region bookkeeping of Dutch-flag partitioning.

name: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference
description: Partition a 2n-length array into two arrays of size n each so that the absolute difference of their sums is minimized.
why_hard: Requires splitting the array into two balanced halves via meet-in-the-middle, then two-pointer scanning across sorted subset-sum lists to find the closest complementary partition — a genuine in-place partition-search problem at Hard difficulty.

name: Constrained Subsequence Sum
description: Choose a subsequence where consecutive chosen indices are at most k apart, maximizing the sum of the subsequence.
why_hard: A DP where `dp[i] = a[i] + max(0, dp[i-k..i-1])` must be computed online, which is only fast with a monotonic deque holding the best dp value in the trailing window — a genuine deque-optimized DP.

name: Watching Fireworks is Fun
description: You move along a street of n sections at speed ≤ d; for each of m fireworks launched at position a_i giving happiness b_i − |a_i − x|, choose your position over time to maximize total happiness.
why_hard: The DP transition for each firework is a sliding-window maximum over the previous DP row (window width grows with d·Δt), so the O(n·m) DP only becomes efficient once you maintain the window max with a monotonic deque.

name: Pictures with Kittens (hard version)
description: Choose exactly x pictures from n so that every window of k consecutive pictures contains at least one chosen picture, maximizing total beauty of chosen pictures.
why_hard: The 2D DP `dp[i][j]` (best value picking j pictures from first i, last chosen within k of i) needs a sliding-window maximum over a fixed-size range per layer, a standard but non-trivial monotonic-deque DP optimization.

name: Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals
description: Design a data structure that, given a stream of integers, can add a value and return the current set of disjoint intervals covering all values seen so far.
why_hard: Requires an online insert-and-merge-interval routine (find neighboring intervals to merge with a new point, splice them together) that must stay efficient across repeated insertions rather than a one-shot batch merge.

name: Range Module
description: Design a data structure to track ranges of integers, supporting adding a range, removing a range, and querying whether every integer in a range is currently tracked, with ranges auto-merging.
why_hard: A direct generalization of "merge intervals" into a full mutable interval-set data structure supporting add/remove/query, forcing careful handling of partial overlaps and interval splitting, not just a static merge.

name: Count Integers in Intervals
description: Design a data structure that supports adding an interval of integers and querying the total count of distinct integers currently covered by all added intervals (with automatic merging of overlaps).
why_hard: Maintaining a dynamically merged set of intervals while tracking total covered length under repeated insertions is a harder, stateful version of the static "merge intervals" exercise.

name: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
description: Given a list of intervals and a list of query points, for each query find the size of the smallest interval that contains it.
why_hard: Requires sorting intervals and queries together and sweeping with a min-heap keyed by interval size, a technique that builds directly on interval-sorting fundamentals but adds an offline sweep over queries.

name: The Union of k-Segments
description: Given n segments and an integer k, find the minimal set of disjoint segments whose union is exactly the set of points covered by at least k of the input segments.
why_hard: Combines a coverage-counting sweep (via segment endpoint events) with merging the resulting "covered ≥ k times" points back into a minimal list of maximal merged segments.

name: Counting Kangaroos is Fun
description: Given n kangaroo sizes, a kangaroo can hide inside another's pocket only if the holder is at least twice its size (each kangaroo can hold at most one, and a held kangaroo can't itself hold another); minimize the number of visible kangaroos.
why_hard: After sorting, the optimal strategy greedily pairs the smallest unmatched kangaroo with the smallest kangaroo in the upper half able to hold it, advancing two pointers from the middle outward — the two-pointer greedy needs a matching-theory argument to prove optimality, not just intuition.

name: Eugene and an array
description: Count the number of nonempty subarrays of an array (values may be negative) in which every one of its own subarrays has a nonzero sum, i.e., subarrays with no internal zero-sum stretch.
why_hard: A subarray is "good" exactly when its prefix sums are pairwise distinct, so for each right endpoint the left boundary must stay past the most recent repeated prefix sum; maintaining that boundary with a hashmap of last-seen prefix sums turns a seemingly combinatorial zero-sum-subarray condition into a monotonic two-pointer sweep.

name: Count Triangles
description: Given A ≤ B ≤ C ≤ D, count integer-sided non-degenerate triangles (x, y, z) with A ≤ x ≤ B ≤ y ≤ C ≤ z ≤ D.
why_hard: The only binding triangle inequality is z < x + y, so the count of valid z for a pair (x, y) is a simple range length; summing that over all O((B−A)(C−B)) pairs directly is too slow, so the trick is a two-pointer sweep over x and y where the z-threshold moves monotonically, letting you accumulate the answer in linear time.

name: 1D Sokoban
description: Starting at position 0 on an infinite line with n boxes and m special positions, you can walk left/right and any boxes in your path get pushed along with you (never pulled); choose your movements to maximize the number of boxes ending on special positions.
why_hard: Pushed boxes compact together, so walking to some farthest point R on one side always leaves the boxes there stacked at consecutive positions ending at R, collapsing the search to one free "how far right" and one free "how far left" parameter; matching the resulting compressed positions against the sorted special positions with two pointers, then combining a right-then-left pass with a left-then-right pass, is the non-obvious part.

name: Robin Hood
subtopic: binary search on answer + prefix sums (sorted array)
description: Given n citizens' coin counts and k days, where each day one coin moves from a current richest citizen to a current poorest citizen, compute the gap between the richest and poorest amounts after k days.
why_hard: Simulating up to 10^9 days directly is impossible, so the trick is binary searching independently on the final minimum and maximum values and using prefix sums over the sorted array to compute, in O(1), how many coin-moves are needed to lift everyone up to a candidate floor (or cap everyone at a candidate ceiling) within the day budget.
